nodes.label: Spatial history / Historical geography
nodes.date_label: Sauer 1925 · Hoskins 1955 · critical spatial studies and historical GIS by the 1990s · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Investigates how places, landscapes, territories and spatial relationships are made and transformed through time. Reconstructing past geographies, interpreting maps and colonial naming, tracing contested place identities, and linking historical records through GIS are different practices within this broad field.

nodes.scope_note: Historical geography has roots well before digital mapping. Spatial history is an overlapping set of approaches, not a synonym for GIS or one unified school. The existing Geography & environmental inquiry entry retains its wider intellectual resources. This selection foregrounds British reconstruction, Australian colonial space and a British HGIS project; wider regional traditions and Indigenous spatial knowledge require fuller treatment. Later digital projects are not backdated into coverage through 2000.

strands.title: Landscape reconstruction and historical traces
strands.focus: Sauer’s morphological programme and Hoskins’s landscape reading offer distinct ways of studying past environments.

strands.title: Reconstructing geography from historical records
strands.focus: Darby works from Domesday evidence; the extent of a source is not identical to the geography of a whole society.

strands.title: Maps as historical representations
strands.focus: Harley asks how power, rhetoric and conventions enter mapmaking. His argument supplies source criticism, not a reason to abandon spatial measurement.

strands.title: Contested places and their pasts
strands.focus: Massey’s relational account appears alongside Driver and Samuel’s spatial-history editorial; co-publication does not imply one shared theory.

strands.title: Colonial naming and spatial narratives
strands.focus: Carter examines Australian territorial representation; this analysis must remain distinct from Indigenous authority over Country.

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public interpretation
strands.focus: Hayden links material places with histories of diverse urban lives.

strands.title: Historical GIS (HGIS) and changing boundaries
strands.focus: Gregory and Southall’s 1998 account links changing administrative units with historical statistics; proposed extensions remain proposals.

nodes.label: Intellectual history
nodes.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.

nodes.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.

nodes.label: Labour history
nodes.date_label: Webbs 1894/1920 · Thompson 1963 · expanding comparative and feminist inquiries in the 1970s–1990s · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Studies work, workers, labour relations and collective organisation across paid, unpaid, coerced, agricultural and industrial settings. Labour history includes unions and politics, workplace authority, household economies, culture, race, gender and colonial categories. Labour and labor are spelling variants; neither social history nor British Marxism exhausts the field.

nodes.scope_note: Institutional histories, Marxist cultural analysis, feminist inquiry and colonial labour studies coexist and disagree. Thompson’s work already contains a cultural reorientation; later gender analysis involves productive inheritance as well as criticism. This selection includes Britain, the United States, France, South Asia and Africa but does not constitute global coverage. Labour institutions and historical scholarship about them have different chronologies. Fuller Latin American, Caribbean, East Asian and Indigenous labour historiographies remain priorities.

strands.focus: Kumar scrutinizes categories; Chakrabarty’s Bengal interpretation receives Nair’s criticism; Cooper studies African labour politics. These cases do not share one model.

nodes.label: Ethnohistory
nodes.date_label: Earlier interdisciplinary work · Great Lakes–Ohio Valley project 1953 · Lurie 1961 · continuing regional programmes · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Combines historical and anthropological inquiry through archives, material evidence, language, oral traditions and situated cultural interpretation. North American claims research, Wendat/Huron historical reconstruction, Nahua documentary studies and Andean historical anthropology form distinct programmes. Ethnohistory studies historical change rather than assigning some peoples to an unchanging ethnographic past.

nodes.scope_note: The field overlaps with Indigenous history but does not automatically confer Indigenous authority, community consent or decolonizing method. Claims research could serve governments as well as claimants. Indigenous authors appear here as qualified interlocutors and critics, not as members of an externally assigned school. Lurie herself disputes restricting the approach to particular peoples. The Americas dominate this initial selection; Vansina provides a comparison with African oral-tradition methodology, not proof that African history descends from US ethnohistory.

strands.title: Ethnological reading and documentary criticism
strands.focus: Lurie questions special-people definitions and examines the conditions under which documents were produced.

strands.title: Archaeology and histories across contact
strands.focus: Trigger’s Wendat/Huron inquiry examines precontact change as well as European encounters.

strands.title: Nahua texts and colonial mediation
strands.focus: Lockhart’s documentary programme makes Indigenous-language writing central; notarial conventions and scribal selection still require criticism.

strands.title: Andean historical anthropology
strands.focus: Murra and Wachtel question static reconstructions and combine fieldwork, historical records and language; Revel shares the editorial project.

strands.title: Collaboration and Indigenous historical authority
strands.focus: The Yukon collaboration, Wilson’s criticism and Rivera’s account of collective practice pose different questions about who interprets and controls knowledge.
strands.works: Life Lived Like a Story (1990); Wilson (1996); Rivera (1987)

strands.title: Oral tradition as a comparative methodological problem
strands.focus: Vansina’s analysis of transmission supplies a comparison with documentary interpretation; oral traditions and retrospective interviews are not identical sources.

verification.note: Read frontmatter, contents, full preface ix–x and introduction 1–3 in PDF text; later introduction and essays unread. Imprint distinguishes 1978 collection, 1986 translation and 2009 reprint. Coeditorship, source criticism and interdisciplinary programme supported; no complete Andean survey or empirical validation claimed.

edges.relationship: Sauer: reconstructing cultural landscapes
edges.evidence_note: A specific geographical programme provides one resource; historical geography is not reduced to environmental determination.
edges.map_label: Sauer: reconstructing cultural landscapes

edges.relationship: Driver and Samuel: the 1995 spatial-history forum
edges.evidence_note: Coeditorship and Massey’s accompanying intervention document a particular forum; the unread editorial body is not assigned a detailed argument.
edges.map_label: Driver and Samuel: the 1995 spatial-history forum

edges.relationship: Harley: power and cartographic knowledge
edges.evidence_note: Harley explicitly draws on Foucault, alongside a distinct Derridean resource. This names a reception, not Foucault as founder of historical geography.
edges.map_label: Harley: power and cartographic knowledge

edges.relationship: Harley: rhetoric and textuality of maps
edges.evidence_note: Harley acknowledges an eclectic combination of partly incompatible ideas; the edge records this particular use.
edges.map_label: Harley: rhetoric and textuality of maps

edges.relationship: Gregory and Southall: statistics across changing boundaries
edges.evidence_note: The 1998 HGIS abstract describes a spatial framework for historical statistics. It supports a methodological contribution, not validation of every quantitative result.
edges.map_label: Gregory and Southall: statistics across changing boundaries

edges.relationship: Hayden: interpreting urban places
edges.evidence_note: One documented landscape project connects spatial interpretation with urban history.
edges.map_label: Hayden: interpreting urban places

edges.relationship: Carter: colonial naming and territorial narratives
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of a specific Australian spatial inquiry with postcolonial questions; no reception by a named postcolonial theorist is inferred.
edges.map_label: Carter: colonial naming and territorial narratives

edges.relationship: Skinner, Pocock and Brett: contextual inquiries
edges.evidence_note: Named approaches contribute to a wider field without defining it or subsuming every intellectual historian.
edges.map_label: Skinner, Pocock and Brett: contextual inquiries

edges.relationship: Koselleck: concepts and historical temporalities
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary passages distinguish semantic inquiry from direct reduction to social structures.
edges.map_label: Koselleck: concepts and historical temporalities

edges.relationship: LaCapra: texts and their contexts
edges.evidence_note: Publisher-supported scope of one methodological project, not a claim that intellectual history uniformly accepted poststructuralism. Toews’s detailed intervention remains unread.
edges.map_label: LaCapra: texts and their contexts

edges.relationship: Darnton: material circulation of Enlightenment ideas
edges.evidence_note: Publishing and distribution connect intellectual and cultural questions in a named project; neither field is claimed to descend from the other.
edges.map_label: Darnton: material circulation of Enlightenment ideas

edges.relationship: Maruyama: thought and Japanese transformation
edges.evidence_note: A comparison of explanatory questions; no institutional or intellectual affiliation with the modernization-theory entry is asserted.
edges.map_label: Maruyama: thought and Japanese transformation

edges.relationship: Thompson: class formation and work discipline
edges.evidence_note: Primary preface and selected article passages support a cultural and relational inquiry, not a noncultural class model.
edges.map_label: Thompson: class formation and work discipline

edges.relationship: Dorothy Thompson: Chartism and women’s politics
edges.evidence_note: Distinct historical work and agency; not merely an incidental cross-link through her husband.
edges.map_label: Dorothy Thompson: Chartism and women’s politics

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm: labour movements and working lives
edges.evidence_note: A contextual work selection identifies his contribution without equating all labour historians with British Marxism.
edges.map_label: Hobsbawm: labour movements and working lives

edges.relationship: Gutman and Montgomery: work cultures and workplace politics
edges.evidence_note: Gutman credits British resources while criticizing some US New Left labour histories; his 1973 population limit is retained.
edges.map_label: Gutman and Montgomery: work cultures and workplace politics

edges.relationship: Perrot: serial training and strike histories
edges.evidence_note: Retrospective biographical evidence documents supervision and a particular adaptation; Perrot’s later feminist work is not reduced to this training.
edges.map_label: Perrot: serial training and strike histories

edges.relationship: Tilly, Scott and Anna Clark: work, family and gender
edges.evidence_note: Feminist inquiry productively expands and criticizes labour categories; its relation to Thompson is not simple rejection.
edges.map_label: Tilly, Scott and Anna Clark: work, family and gender

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty and Nair: Bengal labour and its critics
edges.evidence_note: Chakrabarty’s inquiry and Nair’s gender/culture criticism identify an internally contested intervention.
edges.map_label: Chakrabarty and Nair: Bengal labour and its critics

edges.relationship: Cooper: work and decolonization
edges.evidence_note: The Mombasa case and colonial labour categories connect research fields through a specified project, not a universal model for Africa.
edges.map_label: Cooper: work and decolonization

edges.relationship: Alice and Staughton Lynd: rank-and-file accounts
edges.evidence_note: Named joint editorial practice connects oral-history methods with workers’ histories; interview selection remains interpretive.
edges.map_label: Alice and Staughton Lynd: rank-and-file accounts

edges.relationship: Lucassen and Zürcher: military labour
edges.evidence_note: The coauthored 1998 comparison connects recruitment with household strategies and labour arrangements.
edges.map_label: Lucassen and Zürcher: military labour

edges.relationship: Work, households and broader social history
edges.evidence_note: An editorial comparison of overlapping questions, not the identity of two fields or an inferred direction of influence.
edges.map_label: Work, households and broader social history

edges.relationship: Lurie: documentary interpretation and ethnological inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Her 1961 methodological argument supplies a specific contribution; its categories and disciplinary claims remain attributed.
edges.map_label: Lurie: documentary interpretation and ethnological inquiry

edges.relationship: Murra, Wachtel and Revel: the Andean collection
edges.evidence_note: The 1978 Annales collection and 1986 translation document an editorial connection, not an Annales origin for Andean scholarship.
edges.map_label: Murra, Wachtel and Revel: the Andean collection

edges.relationship: Historical reconstruction and Indigenous authority
edges.evidence_note: Comparison between the documentary programmes represented here and Wilson’s concerns about historical authority; no universal affiliation or endorsement is inferred.
edges.map_label: Historical reconstruction and Indigenous authority

edges.relationship: Cruikshank and Yukon elders: collaborative life histories
edges.evidence_note: Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned are named contributors alongside Cruikshank; oral history is not simply raw material collected by an academic.
edges.map_label: Cruikshank and Yukon elders: collaborative life histories

edges.relationship: Vansina: comparing oral-tradition methods
edges.evidence_note: Shared methodological questions do not establish a genealogy from US ethnohistory to African historical scholarship.
edges.map_label: Vansina: comparing oral-tradition methods

edges.relationship: Claims research and historical territories
edges.evidence_note: Wheeler-Voegelin’s commissioned project provides a concrete comparison of territorial reconstruction and historical geography, not documented influence on HGIS.
edges.map_label: Claims research and historical territories

preservation: Every earlier node, person, source and edge object is unchanged; all other top-level fields except appended revision history are unchanged, including the entire journal catalogue.
